newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Trial exposes thriving heroin trade in Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: Trial exposes thriving heroin trade in Vietnam.

text.p: The trial of border guards and state security officials in Hanoi for their part in a huge heroin-trafficking racket has highlighted Vietnam's growing role as a transit route for drugs from the notorious Golden Triangle.
Drug experts say the communist country's move to open borders long closed to the outside world, combined with rampant corruption, has brought a bonanza for international dealers.

"Vietnam was relatively protected until a few years ago because the borders were closed and the country was very poor," said Joern Kristensen, head of the United Nations Drug Control Programme (UNDCP) office in Hanoi.
"Now it has emerged as a transit country. It's easier here than in other countries, where they have had this problem for years and law enforcement agencies are well trained."

The UNDCP points to a leap in drug seizures in border areas and at international airports as a sign that traffickers are targetting Vietnam both as a market and a transit route for shipment to North America, Australia and other Asian countries.
In 1991, when the problem was still almost unheard of in Vietnam, authorities seized just 1.5 kg (3.3 pounds) of heroin.
But by 1995 their haul was almost 31 kg (68.2 pounds) and in the first eight months of last year it was 49 kg (108 pounds) -- at wholesale prices in New York, that could sell for around $2.5 million.
Le Duc Hien of the government's Social Evils Prevention Department told Reuters that during 1996, a total of 772 people were charged with drug-trafficking offences in Vietnam in 395 separate cases.
But drug experts say the seizures of heroin brought from the Golden Triangle -- where the borders of Thailand, Laos and Burma meet -- represent just the tip of an iceberg.
The ring broken by this month's trial is alone believed to have brought some 300 kg (660 pounds) of heroin into Vietnam.

The UNDCP says there are several reasons why Vietnam has become an attractive transit country for traffickers, the most important being the large amount of opium -- from which heroin is synthesised -- that is available in neighbouring countries.

Opium production in Vietnam has been slashed to about 10-15 tonnes a year. But annual production in neighbouring Laos is around 200 tonnes and Burma's output, by some estimates, could top 2,500 tonnes a year, making it the world's largest producer.
Vietnam also has long land borders and coastal areas, which are difficult to control, and the government's new push for trade with the outside world has made its borders more porous.

As the latest trial shows, much of the drugs trade has gone unnoticed because the country's poorly paid law enforcement officers sometimes take bribes for turning a blind eye, or even get involved in ferrying consignments themselves.
Vietnam has not yet signed the United Nations conventions on drug trafficking that provide frameworks for exchanging information.
UNDCP's Kristensen says Hanoi is moving in the direction of international cooperation. But it will have to act quickly to catch up with the drug trade's slippery criminals.
